title: Church and State in America
objective: After this level you can explain the First Amendment's two religion clauses and where the idea of a "wall of separation" came from.
summary: Virginia's 1786 statute, the First Amendment's Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses and Article VI set out religious freedom; Jefferson's 1802 letter coined the 'wall of separation'.

cards.headline: America's "wall of separation" isn't written in the Constitution.
cards.body: The famous phrase comes from a president's letter to a group of Baptists. Before the letter, though, come the laws it was describing.

cards.headline: Virginia goes first
cards.body: On January 16, 1786, Virginia enacted its Statute for Religious Freedom. Thomas Jefferson wrote it, and James Madison guided it to passage while Jefferson was abroad. It declared that no one could be compelled to support any religious worship, or suffer for their religious opinions or belief. Jefferson was proud of it: he had his authorship listed on his tombstone.

cards.headline: Two clauses, one sentence
cards.body: The First Amendment, ratified in 1791, begins: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." That holds two clauses. The Establishment Clause bars government from establishing a religion; the Free Exercise Clause protects religious practice. Article VI adds that "no religious Test shall ever be required" for federal office.
cards.callout: Establishment: no official faith. Free exercise: freedom to practice.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. One clause keeps government from backing a faith; the other keeps it from blocking one.

cards.headline: The wall
cards.body: The Danbury Baptist Association of Connecticut wrote to President Jefferson, complaining of religious oppression by their state government. On January 1, 1802, he replied that religion "lies solely between Man & his God", and that the First Amendment built "a wall of separation between Church & State." The idea still echoes. In 1976 the Census Bureau's director said a mandatory religion question would appear to infringe on that separation.

cards.headline: Church and State in America: the takeaways
learned: Virginia's 1786 statute protected freedom of belief
The First Amendment bars an official religion and protects practice
Jefferson's 1802 letter coined the "wall of separation"

questions.prompt: Put these milestones of American religious freedom in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom came in 1786, the First Amendment in 1791, Jefferson's "wall of separation" letter in 1802, and the Census Bureau director's remark in 1976.

questions.prompt: How do the First Amendment's two religion clauses divide the work?

options.label: One protects church buildings; the other exempts them from taxes
options.rationale: Neither clause is about buildings or taxes.

options.label: One bars an official religion; the other protects religious practice
One requires each state to choose a church; the other lets people switch
One covers Christians; the other covers people of all other faiths

questions.explanation: The Establishment Clause bars government from establishing a religion; the Free Exercise Clause protects religious practice.

questions.prompt: Level 9 said the US census may not require answers about religion. What reason did the Census Bureau's director give in 1976?

options.label: Americans have no religious identity to report
It would appear to infringe on the separation of church and state
The First Amendment requires a religion question on the census
Religion questions were too costly to print
options.rationale: He named separation of church and state.

questions.explanation: In 1976 the director said a mandatory religion question would appear to infringe upon the separation of church and state; a 1976 law then barred one.
